title: Condition
subtitle: unless, provided that, in case of, whatever
summary: Express conditions with more precision than if, using unless, provided that, in case of, -ever words and condition nouns.

lesson.heading: Words connecting sentence parts
rows: unless
You can't come in **unless** you have a ticket.
= if you do not have a ticket
on condition that
You can borrow the bike **on condition that** you return it by five o'clock.
the strongest and most restricting
provided / providing (that)
**Provided** you don't mind cats, you can stay with us.
less formal than on condition that, but stronger than as long as
as / so long as
You can stay, **as long as** you don't mind sleeping on the sofa.
the least formal and least strong
in case of / in the event of
**In case of** fire, dial 112.
usually seen on notices

lesson.heading: in case of and in case

left.label: in case of = when there is
left.text: **In case of** introduces a situation that may happen; it is the language of notices and regulations.
examples: **In the event of** an emergency, sound the alarm.

right.label: in case = because it might
right.text: **In case** explains a precaution you take now because something might happen later.
examples: Take your umbrella **in case** it rains.
Take a jacket **in case** it gets cold later on.

lesson.note: Take your umbrella in case it rains means 'It isn't raining but it might rain.'

lesson.heading: Supposing ... and What if ...
lesson.text: **Supposing** and **what if** introduce a possible future situation. Both belong mainly to spoken English; **what if** is the more direct of the two.

examples.text: *Mick:* Ethan's coming tomorrow. He'll help us. *Alice:* **Supposing** he doesn't turn up - what shall we do then?
**What if** the train is late? We'll miss the connection.
**Supposing** I lent you my car, would that help?

lesson.heading: Conditions with -ever
lesson.text: The suffix **-ever** means 'it does not matter which'. The stress falls on *ever*. Each of these can be replaced by **no matter** + question word.

examples.text: **However** you decide to travel in this country, it'll cost you a lot of money.
You'll end up paying at least 70 euros, **whichever** means of transport you take.
Public transport is expensive **wherever** you go here.
**Whoever** wins the next election should try to lower fares.

lesson.heading: -ever and no matter
rows: **Wherever** she goes, she takes her dog.
**No matter where** she goes, she takes her dog.
**Whatever** I do, I do the wrong thing.
**No matter what** I do, I do the wrong thing.
**Whoever** it is, I won't speak to them.
**No matter who** it is, I won't speak to them.
**However** hard you try, you can't do it alone.
**No matter how** hard you try, you can't do it alone.

lesson.heading: Nouns which express condition
lesson.text: These nouns are rather formal and belong mostly to written or official English. A **prerequisite** is something absolutely necessary before you can do something else.

examples.text: Certain **conditions** must be met before the peace talks can begin.
A good standard of English is a **prerequisite** for studying at a British university.
What are the entry **requirements** for a diploma in Management?
I would not move to London under any **circumstances**.

lesson.text: After these condition expressions use a present tense, never will: Take a jacket in case it gets cold later on, not ~~in case it will get cold~~.

exercises.prompt: You can't come in ___ you have a ticket.
___ emergency in the machine room, sound the alarm and notify the supervisor at once.
exercises.explanation: In case of / In the event of = when there is; typical of notices and regulations.

exercises.prompt: ___ I hear from you, I'll assume you are coming.
exercises.explanation: Unless I hear from you = if I do not hear from you.

exercises.prompt: ___ I lent you my car, would that help?
exercises.explanation: Supposing and What if introduce a possible situation; both are mainly spoken.

exercises.prompt: A person may take the driving test again ___ they have not already taken a test within the previous 14 days.
exercises.explanation: On condition that is the strongest and suits legal or official language.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with -ever: 'No matter where she goes, she always takes that dog of hers.' ___ she goes, she always takes that dog of hers.
Rewrite with -ever: 'If anyone rings, I don't want to speak to them, no matter who it is.' ... I don't want to speak to them, ___ it is.
Rewrite with -ever: 'No matter what I do, I always seem to do the wrong thing.' ___ I do, I always seem to do the wrong thing.
Rewrite with no matter: 'However hard you try, you'll never be able to do it all on your own.'
options: No matter how hard you try, ...
No matter what hard you try, ...
No matter which hard you try, ...

exercises.prompt: 'Take your umbrella in case it rains' means:
options: It isn't raining now but it might rain.
It is raining, so take the umbrella.
You may only go out if it rains.
It never rains, so leave the umbrella.
exercises.explanation: In case explains a precaution against something that might happen.

exercises.statement: Take a jacket in case it will get cold later on.
exercises.explanation: Take a jacket in case it gets cold later on. Use a present tense after in case, never will.

exercises.prompt: A notice at a mosque. Put the words in order.
exercises.answer: Visitors may enter the mosque on condition that they remove their shoes.
exercises.explanation: On condition that is the strongest and most official condition word.

exercises.prompt: Which expressions belong to formal or official English, and which are everyday spoken English?
